Code Eric Granger Affiliation: LIVIA, École de technologie supérieure Abstract Person re-identification (ReID) ranks an image gallery using either an image query or a textual query. In image-to-image (I2I) ReID, viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, and background changes can make distractors appear more similar than the true match. In text-to-image (T2I) ReID, incomplete or ambiguous descriptions may omit key visual evidence. We study this problem for vision-language model (VLM) based ReID, where attributes such as clothing color and carried objects provide useful fine-grained matching cues. However, directly using attribute-prompt similarities as retrieval scores is unreliable because templated prompts can be biased, correlated, and poorly calibrated. We therefore propose PR ompt-guided A ttribute-based I nference-time S imilarity E nhancement ( PRAISE ), a query-side test-time adaptation framework for VLM-based ReID. Instead of treating prompts as scores, PRAISE uses a transferable attribute-prompt bank to construct an Attribute-Conditioned Subspace (ACS): a query-dependent low-rank subspace induced by the most compatible attribute prompts. ACS provides a controlled attribute-conditioned geometry for reshaping query–gallery affinities and guiding lightweight inference-time updates without identity or attribute labels. Experiments across multiple I2I- and T2I-ReID benchmarks show that PRAISE consistently improves VLM retrieval backbones and outperforms both generic and ReID-specific TTA baselines. Figure 1 : Motivation and overview of PRAISE . (a) In I2I-ReID, raw visual similarity can retrieve distractors caused by camera, pose, or background bias. (b) In T2I-ReID, incomplete text descriptions can produce partial matches that share only some mentioned attributes. (c) PRAISE addresses both cases by selecting query-relevant attribute directions, orthogonalizing them into an Attribute-Conditioned Subspace (ACS), and using this controlled subspace to reshape query-gallery affinities during test-time. 1 Introduction Person re-identification (ReID) aims to retrieve images of the same identity across cameras and time. It is commonly studied in two retrieval settings: image-to-image (I2I) ReID, where an image query is matched against an image gallery, and text-to-image (T2I) ReID, where a natural-language description is used to retrieve the corresponding person image. Despite steady progress in both settings using image and text supervision [ 26 , 55 ] , test-time retrieval remains sensitive to nuisance factors. In I2I-ReID, viewpoint changes, pose variation, blur, illumination, occlusion, and background clutter can make visually plausible distractors outrank the true match [ 38 ] . In T2I-ReID, retrieval can fail for a complementary reason: natural-language descriptions are often incomplete, ambiguous, or noisy, and may omit discriminative visual evidence [ qin2024noisy ] . Thus, although the query modality differs, both settings suffer from insufficiently reliable query-gallery evidence at test time. A natural way to strengthen this evidence is to use semantic attributes as an auxiliary matching signal. If a query and a gallery image depict the same identity, their match should be supported not only by raw embedding similarity, but also by agreement over stable person-centric cues such as clothing color, clothing type, carried objects, hair, or accessories. Conversely, if two samples correspond to different identities, at least some of these cues are likely to disagree. We refer to such cues as attributes : attributes that are visually observable, likely to remain meaningful across camera views, and expressible in both image and text queries. These attributes are not intended to uniquely identify a person, but they can provide useful corrective evidence for rejecting implausible matches and reinforcing plausible ones. Attribute-based cues have been widely explored in person retrieval, including attribute-based ReID and text-based person search [ 42 , 49 , 12 , 5 ] . Prior methods typically use attributes as predicted labels, auxiliary supervision, or learned cross-modal embeddings, relying on training or fine-tuning to calibrate visual evidence with attribute semantics. In contrast, our work considers a more realistic setting in which no target-domain identity labels or attribute annotations are available, and no additional attribute classifier can be trained. Under these constraints, we construct a transferable bank of attributes that capture visually observable, person-centric cues, such as clothing color and type, hair, and accessories, that remain stable across camera views and can be consistently expressed in both image and text queries. VLMs [ 26 , 14 , 55 ] can encode these cues as natural-language prompts, allowing textual semantics to be reused in I2I-ReID, where the text branch is typically discarded at inference [ 26 ] , while naturally supporting T2I-ReID. A simple approach is to compare query and gallery responses to this prompt bank and fuse the resulting attribute similarity with identity affinity. However, we show that this direct fusion is unreliable because attribute prompts are coarse, shared across identities, correlated in VLM text space, and biased by prompt templates. Consequently, raw attribute scores are often poorly calibrated and can amplify generic distractors instead of improving retrieval. This motivates a different test-time use of attributes. Instead of acting as direct matching scores, prompts should guide the adaptation geometry itself. To this end, we propose PRAISE : PR ompt-guided A ttribute-based I nference-time S imilarity E nhancement. For each query, PRAISE selects the most compatible attribute prompts and orthogonalizes their directions to form an Attribute-Conditioned Subspace (ACS). Query-gallery comparisons are then reshaped within this low-rank, query-conditioned subspace, allowing attributes to provide structured auxiliary evidence without relying on brittle prompt-profile matching. The resulting ACS affinity is combined with the standard identity affinity and used to drive a lightweight test-time adaptation objective that updates only normalization parameters. We assume a transductive retrieval setting where the gallery is available at test time, following prior works [ adachi2024test , wang2020tent ] . The same mechanism applies to both I2I-ReID and T2I-ReID, differing only in whether the query representation is produced by the visual or text encoder. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) PRAISE , a test-time adaptation method for ReID that improves query-gallery ranking by combining identity affinity with prompt-guided attribute evidence while updating only lightweight normalization parameters. (2) The Attribute-Conditioned Subspace (ACS), a test-time-compatible mechanism that uses attribute prompts as query-conditioned geometric directions rather than direct matching scores, mitigating prompt-similarity bias during retrieval. (3) A label-free, transferable attribute prompt-bank construction protocol for ReID. The bank captures stable person-centric cues, is pre-encoded once, requires no target-domain identity or attribute labels, and supports both I2I and T2I retrieval. 2 Related Works Image-to-Image (I2I) Re-identification. I2I-ReID methods were developed as the principal form of Re-identification in different scenarios such as ordinary/traditional ReID [ 8 , 16 , 48 , 37 ] , clothes-changing ReID [ 23 , 24 , 6 , 11 ] , Visual Infrared-ReID [ 41 , 18 , 51 , 50 , 54 , 32 ] for low lighting conditions, etc. Recently, models such as CLIP-ReID [ 26 ] have emerged, which use the superior representation power of VLMs in order to perform Re-identification. General-purpose models such as PLIP [ 55 ] have also been proposed, which are essentially VLMs intended for use in ReID settings for both I2I and T2I (Text-to-image) ReID. However, existing VLM-based ReID methods largely underutilize multimodal alignment by relying on cosine similarity between visual embeddings. We argue that this image-only approach overlooks the text branch as a stable semantic prior for mitigating domain shifts, such as camera bias, pose variation [ 38 ] , and visual noise. Test-time Adaptation of VLMs. Several methods have been proposed to adapt VLMs to unseen data streams. CLIPArTT [ 7 ] introduces a cross-modal pseudo-labeling loss that refines image-wise prompts, while WATT [ 30 ] utilizes prompt ensembling to stabilize retrieval. However, these loss functions often remain heuristically decoupled from the original contrastive geometry of the backbone. Alternative paradigms, such as TPT [ 36 ] , employ prompt tuning to optimize context tokens at test time, but reliance on multiple stochastic augmentations introduces significant computational overhead. Gradient-free alternatives like TDA [ 17 ] utilize cache-based pseudo-labeling to simulate few-shot episodes, yet struggle under severe out-of-distribution shifts where the cached support becomes unreliable. In contrast to classification-centric TTA methods, we propose PRAISE , which modulates adaptation geometry through an attribute-conditioned subspace. By updating only a small set of normalization parameters, PRAISE enables robust open-set adaptation without unstable global updates or costly augmentation-based tuning. Text-to-Image (T2I) Re-identification. Existing T2I-ReID methods [ 4 , 13 , qin2024noisy , 39 , 53 , 44 , 46 ] predominantly follow a tripartite taxonomy based on architectural design: (i) unimodal alignment via modality-specific encoders (e.g., ResNet [ 9 ] , BERT [ 43 ] ), (ii) zero-shot retrieval using general-purpose vision-language models like CLIP [ 35 ] , and (iii) domain-specific multimodal pre-training tailored for ReID. While recent advancements in cross-modal embedding models have bridged the high-level semantic gap, these offline frameworks remain constrained by a static internal knowledge base, making them brittle against dynamic or underspecified text queries during inference. Recent literature has explored interactive paradigms, such as THI [ 34 ] , which utilizes multi-round visual question answering with MLLMs to refine query intent. However, these methods often incur high computational cost and suffer from label leakage or error accumulation. In contrast, PRAISE uses an attribute-conditioned subspace (ACS), aligning visual features with textual prompts via lightweight normalization updates. This enables efficient open-set adaptation without multi-round refinement. 3 Background: Attribute-Guided Retrieval Notation. Denoting as 𝒟 g = { ( x j , p j , c j ) } j = 1 N g \mathcal{D}_{g}\,{=}\,\{(x_{j},p_{j},c_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N_{g}} the gallery where x j x_{j} is a gallery image, p j p_{j} is a person label and c j c_{j} is a camera label 1 1 1 The labels are only denoted for completeness, and are only used for evaluation , we precompute gallery embeddings: 𝐙 g = ℱ v ​ ( 𝐗 g ) ∈ ℝ N g × d \mathbf{Z}_{g}\,{=}\,\mathcal{F}_{v}(\mathbf{X}_{g})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{g}\times d} , where each row 𝐳 g , j \mathbf{z}_{g,j} is ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized. In practice, 𝐙 g \mathbf{Z}_{g} is cached offline, once per test set, to avoid excessive computational loads. Next, let 𝒫 = { s ℓ } ℓ = 1 L \mathcal{P}\,{=}\,\{s_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} be a bank of attribute prompts spanning multiple attribute categories. The specific design of the prompt bank will be discussed later. Encoded prompts are denoted as 𝐙 t = ℱ t ​ ( 𝒫 ) ∈ ℝ L × d \mathbf{Z}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathcal{P})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} with a row-wise ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalization. The central goal of ReID is to rank a gallery for a given query such that images of the same identity appear near the top of the list. In most modern VLM-based pipelines, this is done by comparing normalized embeddings from a visual encoder ℱ v \mathcal{F}_{v} and/or text encoder ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} . For a query ( x i x_{i} , image or text), the query representation is obtained as 𝐳 i = ℱ v ​ ( x i ) \mathbf{z}_{i}=\mathcal{F}_{v}(x_{i}) or 𝐳 i = ℱ t ​ ( x i ) \mathbf{z}_{i}=\mathcal{F}_{t}(x_{i}) depending on query modality. Gallery images are encoded as 𝐙 g = ℱ v ​ ( 𝐗 g ) \mathbf{Z}_{g}=\mathcal{F}_{v}(\mathbf{X}_{g}) , where each row 𝐳 g , j \mathbf{z}_{g,j} corresponds to one gallery image. The standard retrieval affinity is then computed by cosine similarity: 𝐀 id ​ [ i , j ] = 𝐳 ~ i ⊤ ​ 𝐳 ~ g , j , \mathbf{A}_{\text{id}}[i,j]=\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{g,j}, (1) where 𝐳 ~ = 𝐳 / ( ‖ 𝐳 ‖ 2 + ϵ ) \tilde{\mathbf{z}}=\mathbf{z}/(\|\mathbf{z}\|_{2}+\epsilon) . This identity score is simple and effective, but it is also vulnerable to nuisance factors such as viewpoint, illumination, camera style, background clutter, occlusion, and incomplete textual descriptions. These factors can cause visually plausible distractors to receive high similarity even when they do not share the same identity. 3.1 Attribute Scores as Corrective Retrieval Signal A natural way to improve retrieval robustness is to introduce semantic attributes as an additional source of evidence. Attributes such as clothing color, sleeve length, lower-body clothing type, gender, hair, carried objects, and accessories are not sufficient to uniquely identify a person, but they often provide useful constraints on whether a query-gallery pair is plausible. Following this intuition, an established design pattern is score fusion [ 1 , 21 ] . The retrieval system computes two affinities for each query-gallery pair: an identity or appearance affinity 𝐀 id \mathbf{A}_{\text{id}} , and an attribute-based affinity 𝐀 att \mathbf{A}_{\text{att}} . The final matching score is then formed as a weighted combination: 𝐀 ⁡ [ i , j ] = 𝐀 id ​ [ i , j ] + λ att ​ 𝐀 att ​ [ i , j ] , \mathbf{A}[i,j]=\mathbf{A}_{\text{id}}[i,j]+\lambda_{\mathrm{att}}\mathbf{A}_{\text{att}}[i,j], (2) where λ att ≥ 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{att}}\geq 0 controls the contribution of the attribute branch. Conceptually, 𝐀 id \mathbf{A}_{\text{id}} captures the raw embedding-level similarity between the query and gallery image, while 𝐀 att \mathbf{A}_{\text{att}} acts as a corrective semantic score. The identity score can come from an existing ReID backbone, while the attribute score can be computed using an auxiliary attribute classifier, a text-attribute model, or a VLM prompt bank. A high attribute score should promote candidates that share query-consistent semantic evidence, while a low attribute score should suppress candidates whose appearance similarity is likely caused by nuisance correlations. Let 𝒫 = { s ℓ } ℓ = 1 L \mathcal{P}\,{=}\,\{s_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} denote a bank of natural-language attribute prompts, where each prompt describes one semantic attribute, for example ‘‘a photo of a person wearing a red shirt’’ or ‘‘a photo of a person carrying a backpack’’ . These prompts are encoded by the text encoder: 𝐙 t = ℱ t ​ ( 𝒫 ) ∈ ℝ L × d , \mathbf{Z}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathcal{P})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}, (3) with row-wise ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalization to get 𝐙 ¯ t \bar{\mathbf{Z}}_{t} . For a query embedding 𝐳 i \mathbf{z}_{i} , its similarity to the attribute bank is 𝐮 i = 𝐙 ¯ t ​ 𝐳 i ⊤ ∈ ℝ L \mathbf{u}_{i}=\bar{\mathbf{Z}}_{t}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{L} . Similarly, for a gallery embedding 𝐳 g , j \mathbf{z}_{g,j} , its attribute similarity profile is 𝐯 j = 𝐙 ¯ t ​ 𝐳 g , j ⊤ ∈ ℝ L \mathbf{v}_{j}=\bar{\mathbf{Z}}_{t}\mathbf{z}_{g,j}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{L} . The vectors 𝐮 i \mathbf{u}_{i} and 𝐯 j \mathbf{v}_{j} can be interpreted as soft attribute profiles. Each dimension measures how compatible the query or gallery sample is with one prompt in the attribute bank. Therefore, if the query and gallery image correspond to the same identity, one may expect their attribute profiles to be similar. This leads to a direct attribute similarity: 𝐀 att direct ​ [ i , j ] = 𝐮 ~ i ⊤ ​ 𝐯 ~ j , \mathbf{A}_{\text{att}}^{\text{direct}}[i,j]=\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{j}, (4) where 𝐮 ~ i = 𝐮 i / ( ‖ 𝐮 i ‖ 2 + ϵ ) \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{i}\,{=}\,\mathbf{u}_{i}/(\|\mathbf{u}_{i}\|_{2}+\epsilon) and 𝐯 ~ j = 𝐯 j / ( ‖ 𝐯 j ‖ 2 + ϵ ) \tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{j}\,{=}\,\mathbf{v}_{j}/(\|\mathbf{v}_{j}\|_{2}+\epsilon) . In this view, 𝐀 att direct ​ [ i , j ] \mathbf{A}_{\text{att}}^{\text{direct}}[i,j] measures whether the query and gallery induce similar responses over the same set of attribute prompts. It is a query-gallery similarity computed not in the original image/text embedding space, but in the prompt-response space. The appeal of this construction is that it converts attributes into a retrieval-compatible score without requiring explicit attribute labels. It also applies to both I2I and T2I ReID. In I2I ReID, both 𝐮 i \mathbf{u}_{i} and 𝐯 j \mathbf{v}_{j} are obtained by comparing image embeddings to text prompts. In T2I ReID, 𝐮 i \mathbf{u}_{i} is obtained from a text-query embedding and 𝐯 j \mathbf{v}_{j} from a gallery-image embedding, but both are still expressed as responses to the same prompt bank. Thus, direct attribute similarity provides a unified mechanism for using semantic attributes across both retrieval settings. 3.2 Calibration of Prompt-Response Similarity Although direct attribute similarity offers a simple auxiliary retrieval score, it assumes that prompt activations form a reliable matching space. This is unsuitable for ReID because: (1) Identity Closeness: coarse attributes (e.g., “dark hair”) are shared by many identities and are not identity-specific; (2) Template Bias: responses may reflect shared prompt templates rather than visual evidence; e.g., “a photo of a person wearing a red shirt” and “a photo of a person wearing a blue shirt” differ only in the color token but share almost the entire sentence structure. [ 2 , 31 ] (3) Attribute Collision: semantically close captions can produce highly correlated activations; e.g., red / pink / magenta , pants / trousers / long pants , or bag / backpack / shoulder bag [ 15 , 40 ] . As a result, 𝐀 att direct \mathbf{A}_{\text{att}}^{\text{direct}} may have a narrow or poorly structured distribution, making true matches and distractors hard to separate and misaligning it with the raw identity affinity 𝐀 id \mathbf{A}_{\text{id}} . This behavior is illustrated in Figure 2 . The direct attribute-derived affinity exhibits a markedly different distribution from the baseline identity affinity, indicating weak agreement between the two matching views. Under such mismatch, additive fusion becomes unstable: the attribute term is intended to correct 𝐀 id \mathbf{A}_{\text{id}} , but can instead amplify distractors that merely share generic attributes with the query. (a) Without ACS (b) With ACS Figure 2 : Similarity distributions for matching and non-matching query-gallery pairs on Market-1501. Direct prompt-profile similarity (a) is saturated for both groups, whereas ACS (b) yields clearer separation between matches and distractors. This suggests that attribute prompts should not be used as unconstrained scoring functions. Instead, they should define a more controlled comparison space in which identity-level affinity remains the primary signal, while prompt-template bias is reduced and correlated attribute captions are prevented from dominating the score. Such a formulation would preserve the corrective value of attributes without allowing coarse or colliding prompt responses to destabilize retrieval. 4 Attribute conditioned subspace construction and PRAISE Given a frozen VLM and a target-domain test set (queries and gallery), we propose PRAISE , a TTA method that leverages noisy natural-language attribute prompts to recalibrate the embedding space under domain shift to improve query-gallery ranking for both I2I-ReID and T2I-ReID. PRAISE is a TTA method that performs the following key steps: (1) precompute a bank of attribute prompt embeddings, (2) construct a query-conditioned attribute subspace using the prompt bank, and (3) adapt a small subset of backbone parameters at test time, to improve retrieval performance. Please refer to Figure 3 for an overview of the methodology. 4.1 Prompt Bank Construction The quality of the attribute bank is important because PRAISE relies on prompt-induced semantic directions rather than supervised attribute labels. We therefore construct 𝒫 \mathcal{P} through a data-driven but label-free procedure that extracts recurring pedestrian attributes while keeping the vocabulary compact and reproducible. • Captioning. We use Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct [ 47 ] to generate short person-centric descriptions for pedestrian images. The dataset can be any standard ReID dataset. These descriptions are used only to mine recurring attributes, not as identity annotations. • Attribute grouping. We map the generated descriptions into coarse pedestrian categories, including hair, gender, upper-/lower-body clothing color, clothing type, and accessories. • Vocabulary cleaning. Within each category, we keep unique attribute phrases and remove duplicate or near-identical variants, yielding a compact set of attribute suffixes. Each suffix is inserted into the shared template s ℓ = ‘‘A photo of [ATT]’’ s_{\ell}=\texttt{``A photo of [ATT]''} to form 𝒫 = { s ℓ } ℓ = 1 L \mathcal{P}=\{s_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} . The full suffix list is provided in the Supplementary Material. • Prompt encoding and centering. We encode the bank as 𝐙 t = ℱ t ​ ( 𝒫 ) ∈ ℝ L × d \mathbf{Z}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathcal{P})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} and apply row-wise ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalization. To reduce shared-template bias, we also encode a neutral prompt s 0 s_{0} , e.g., “a photo of a person” , and use centered directions 𝐳 ¯ t , ℓ = 𝐳 t , ℓ − 𝐳 t , 0 \bar{\mathbf{z}}_{t,\ell}=\mathbf{z}_{t,\ell}-\mathbf{z}_{t,0} for ℓ ∈ { 1 , … , L } \ell\in\{1,\dots,L\} . Unless otherwise stated, we mine the attribute bank once from the Market-1501 training split and freeze it for all experiments. The same centered bank 𝐙 ¯ t \bar{\mathbf{Z}}_{t} is reused across all evaluation datasets and is not adapted using target identity labels, target attribute labels, or dataset-specific supervision. The resulting bank should therefore be understood as a fixed, label-free, transferable pedestrian attribute vocabulary rather than a dataset-specific classifier. In the Supplementary Material, we report prompt-bank source ablations showing that PRAISE remains stable when the bank is mined from different ReID datasets. Figure 3 : Method overview. PRAISE uses attribute prompts to construct a query-specific semantic subspace that stabilizes query-side adaptation under domain shift. At test time, it performs query-side episodic TTA with a fixed source-space gallery index. We use MSMT17 [ 45 ] and Market-1501 [ 52 ] for I2I, and CUHK-PEDES [ 25 ] and RSTP-ReID [ 53 ] for T2I. At test time, all methods are given (i) the query (image or text) and (ii) the unlabeled target gallery. We pre-encode all gallery features once and reuse them for all methods for efficiency. Furthermore, we ensure that all methods are granted the same access to unlabeled gallery features under the same episodic/reset protocol as our approach. All runtimes are measured on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (single GPU) with identical implementation settings (batch size, mixed precision), and exclude the one-time cost of gallery feature pre-encoding. A consistent trend is that classifier-oriented TTA methods often degrade performance compared to no-adapt (e.g., TENT/SHOT/SAR/ETA) [ wang2020tent , 27 , 29 , 28 ] , with only minor gains from DeYO [ 20 ] . VLM-based TTA methods [ 36 , 17 ] are more stable, while the strongest baselines are ReID-specific methods such as TEMP [ adachi2024test ] and Norm [ 38 ] . We find that direct score fusion has some limited semantic improvement but the poor calibration leads to a poorer Rank-1. PRAISE substantially improves mAP over all baselines and also yields consistent Rank-1 gains. Although TDA and Norm are faster because they are backpropagation-free, PRAISE provides a strong runtime-accuracy tradeoff. Moreover, since Norm is post-hoc, it can be applied on top of PRAISE with only a 0.3ms/sample overhead, further improving performance.
